title: Arching over ALMA
caption: The Milky Way arching over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way curves across the Chilean desert sky, framing the ALMA antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. Beneath its arc, two smudges mark the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, satellite galaxies of our own. On the ground, an artificial green light illuminates the antennas, contrasting with the natural display overhead.
ALMA sits more than 5000 meters above sea level. At that height the air is dry and thin, which gives an excellent view of the Universe and makes the site ideal for a sensitive instrument like ALMA.

ALMA is not one single telescope. It is made of 66 separate antennas spread over the Chajnantor plateau, and they can be moved. By arranging them in different configurations, astronomers can adjust how finely ALMA resolves the objects it observes.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way's shape and colors and the faint Magellanic Clouds show more strongly than to an observer.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: ALMA's antennas collect millimeter and submillimeter light, which is much longer in wavelength than the visible light captured in this photograph. The Magellanic Clouds, the faint patches below the arc, orbit the Milky Way as its smaller companions.
alt: The Milky Way arches over dish antennas lit green on a desert plateau, with two faint smudges below the arc.
